meta.ogDescription: A traditional Persian proverb, documented by John Chardin in 1711 — not Rousseau, and not Aristotle. Here’s how the misattribution spread.

answer.label: Not Jean-Jacques Rousseau — a Persian proverb
answer.authorDates: Recorded in Europe by 1711 · predates Rousseau (b. 1712)
answer.sourceLine: The line is a condensed English form of a Persian proverb. It was pinned on Rousseau by Jehiel Keeler Hoyt in Hoyt’s New Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations (1922), but it already appears in John Chardin’s Voyages en Perse et autres lieux de l’Orient (1711, p. 175) — a year before Rousseau was born, per Wikiquote.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: Voyages en Perse et autres lieux de l’Orient (Jean Chardin, 1711), p. 175
Hoyt’s New Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations (1922)

source.excerpt: A representative French form of the proverb — “La patience est un arbre dont la racine est amère, et dont les fruits sont très doux” — sits behind the familiar English one-liner “Patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet.” This is the proverb’s commonly circulated wording, not a verbatim transcription of Chardin’s page.
trail: Wikiquote’s Patience page lists the line only as attributed to Rousseau, crediting the attribution to Jehiel Keeler Hoyt’s 1922 cyclopedia.
The Rousseau talk page flags it as “a misattribution by Hoyt” that “appears in Voyages en Perse et autres lieux de l’Orient (John Chardin, 1711, page 175), written a year before Rousseau was born.”
It does not appear among the sourced quotations on the main Jean-Jacques Rousseau Wikiquote page.
Quote sites separately (and just as wrongly) tag it Aristotle, again with no ancient source.
source.excerptNote: The widely shared English version is a compressed paraphrase of the longer proverb; there is no evidence Rousseau ever wrote it.
source.rightsNote: The saying is anonymous folk wisdom — a traditional Persian proverb with no individual author to hold rights. Its earliest print record, Chardin’s Voyages en Perse (1711), and the English wording documented in Hoyt’s cyclopedia (1922) are both well before 1931, so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Jean (John) Chardin
author.heading: Who actually recorded the line
author.metaLine: 1643–1713 · French-British traveller & jeweller who chronicled Persia
author.bio: Sir Jean Chardin was a Huguenot jeweller who spent years in Safavid Persia and published his celebrated Voyages en Perse et autres lieux de l’Orient. He did not coin this saying — he recorded it, as one of the Persian proverbs he gathered. The full proverb runs closer to “patience is a tree whose root is bitter, but whose fruit is very sweet.” His 1711 text puts the line in print a year before Rousseau was even born.

misattribution.heading: A double misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is a magnet quote: a tidy piece of folk wisdom that keeps getting stapled to famous names. Two names dominate — and neither holds up.

items.why: The Rousseau credit traces to Jehiel Keeler Hoyt’s New Cyclopedia of Practical Quotations (1922). But the line already appears in Jean Chardin’s Voyages en Perse (1711, p. 175) — a year before Rousseau was born in 1712 — and it is absent from his sourced works.
Many quote databases list it under Aristotle, but it corresponds to nothing in the Aristotelian corpus; it is the same proverb wearing a different famous label.

misattribution.truthLine: The real source is a traditional Persian proverb, put into print by the traveller Jean Chardin in 1711 — not Rousseau, and not Aristotle.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Rousseau
lead: Rousseau is a natural magnet for aphorisms about virtue and self-mastery, so a proverb praising patience slots neatly beside his name. Once Hoyt’s widely reprinted 1922 dictionary attached the credit, later quote books and websites copied it forward without checking.
The irony is that Chardin’s Persian travelogue was admired by Rousseau’s own generation — but admiring a source is not the same as writing its proverbs.
detailsBody: The circulating English line, “Patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet,” is a compression. The fuller proverb likens patience to a tree whose root is bitter and whose fruit is very sweet — a metaphor typical of Persian and broader Near-Eastern proverb traditions.
context.pull: A proverb wearing a philosopher’s name.
